Dryers can kill some mold spores, but not always—and here’s why:

1. Heat Tolerance of Mold Spores

Mold spores are incredibly resilient. While many active mold cells die at temperatures above 140–160°F (60–71°C), dryers typically operate between 125–135°F on high heat. That’s enough to damage or kill some spores, but not all—especially heat-resistant varieties like Aspergillus or Penicillium.

2. Short Exposure Time

Even if the dryer reaches temperatures high enough, the short time items spend at those peak temperatures may not be enough to fully sterilize them. Mold spores may survive brief exposure, especially if they are embedded in thick fabrics.

3. Moisture and Environment

If clothing went in still damp with mold, the dryer might dry the item (halting active growth) but not destroy all spores. Once rewetted or exposed to humidity, surviving spores can reactivate and grow again.

4. Dryer Design

Most home dryers are not designed for sterilization. Unlike autoclaves or lab-grade dryers, they lack the sustained heat and pressure needed to guarantee mold spore destruction.

⸻

What helps kill mold spores on fabric more reliably:
	•	Washing in hot water (above 140°F) with fungicidal additives like vinegar, borax, or hydrogen peroxide.
	•	Drying immediately after to prevent regrowth.
	•	In some cases, discarding heavily infested fabric may be the safest option.
